The Statue of Liberty. A colossal neoclassical copper statue on Bedloe Island, now Liberty Island, in New York Harbor, a gift from France to the United States dedicated in 1886. Designed by French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi with an iron framework by Gustave Eiffel, it has become the world's most recognizable symbol of freedom, democracy, and American ideals, and a gateway monument greeting millions of immigrants arriving by ship.

The statue stands 93 meters tall, 151 meters including the pedestal, holding a torch aloft in her right hand and a tablet inscribed with the date of American independence, July 4, 1776, in her left. France commissioned the statue as a gift to celebrate American independence and democracy. It was funded by French public donations and arrived disassembled in 1885, requiring American donations to construct the pedestal.

The statue depicts Libertas, the Roman goddess of liberty, rendered in Bartholdi's neoclassical style. It was controversial at its dedication for its radical association with republicanism and freedom in an era of monarchies. Designed by Bartholdi with structural ironwork by Gustave Eiffel, who later designed the Eiffel Tower, it represented a feat of engineering and artistic ambition in the 19th century.

The statue became synonymous with immigration to America, particularly for the millions who arrived through Ellis Island, opened in 1892, though the statue itself predates modern mass immigration and was not initially linked to immigrants. An inscription added later, Emma Lazarus's poem The New Colossus, crystallized the statue's association with immigration: "Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free."

The statue has been vandalized, restored, and closed multiple times for security. It remains one of the most visited monuments in the world and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
